subtitle.text: Moving is never easy.
Moving from a big city like Chicago to a small country village is even harder.
Just ask the Barth children.
"There's nothing to do here!" complained the oldest, named Cy.
"I don't see any shops," whined Anthea, the second eldest.
Among her siblings, her nickname was Panther.
When her younger brother, Bobby, was little, he couldn't say Anthea.
He called her Panther instead, and now the others did too.
"What do you mean, we won't have Internet?"
cried Bobby, looking up at his father.
"Eeek! What's that?" Jane screamed.
A little brown field mouse scurried from under the steps and into the grass.
No one in the family had wanted to move to Aunt Martha's house.
But Father had lost his job, and they had no choice.
"It's only for a short while,"
Mother said, trying to comfort the children as they sat at the kitchen table.
"And there're lots of things to do around here," said Aunt Martha.
"Yeah, like catch grasshoppers?"
Cy said in a rather nasty way.
"Grasshoppers? Where?" screamed Jane.
To make matters worse, Mother and Father left the next morning.
Father had some job interviews in Chicago.
The children stood alone on the steps as the car pulled away.
"Baa, baa," cried the baby happily.
"Oh, Lamb. Nothing makes you sad, does it?" Panther laughed.
Hilary, the baby, got his nickname because the first word he said was "baa," just like a little lamb.
The children didn't want to go back inside the house.
There was nothing to do there.
Behind Aunt Martha's house was a thick forest.
And since no one had a better idea, they set off to explore the woods.
"Look!" Bobby pointed excitedly at a family of raccoons.
"Smell these!" Panther said, as she bent over some colorful flowers.
All day, the children searched the forest for new discoveries.
After a while, they found themselves in a thicket of trees.
"It's awfully dark in here," Panther said in a worried voice.
"Maybe we should go back," Jane added.
"Hey! Look at this!" Cy called out excitedly.
Cy had found an old, dried-up well.
"Can you see anything?"
asked Jane, as they all peered down the well.
"Nope! But there's a funny smell," replied Cy.
"Is there any water?" Bobby asked.
The children stared deeper into the well, their eyes getting wider.
"I wonder if this is a wishing well," said Jane.
"Wait! Look here," said Panther.
Next to the well, Panther had found an old wooden bucket attached to some rope.
"Let's lower this bucket and see what's down there," she said.
"What's she doing?" Bobby said, pointing to Jane.
Jane's eyes were closed, and she was holding onto a coin.
"I'm making a wish," she replied.
She turned around and threw the coin over her shoulder and into the well.
Clink, clink, clonk.
"Ouch!" a voice cried from the well.
"Did you hear that?" whispered Bobby.
"Hello, down there!" Cy shouted.
"Hello, down there!"
his voice echoed inside the well. Then silence.
"I'm sure I heard something," said Bobby.
"Do you think it's an animal?" Jane asked worriedly.
"There's only one way to find out," Cy said excitedly.
He lowered the bucket down the well.
"Can you feel anything?" Panther asked.
"Hurry up, will you?" Bobby said impatiently.
Cy pulled the bucket back up.
It was full of mud, soda cans, an old shoe, and some rocks.
Cy lowered the bucket again several times.
If there was something in the well, he was determined to find it.
After a while, Cy got tired of lowering the bucket.
The others wanted to give up, too.
Cy let out a deep breath.
"That's it. There's nothing else down there,"
he said, emptying a final bucket load.
"Wait," cried Panther.
"Look at this!"
She picked out an unusual shell covered in mud.
"What is it?" Jane asked, looking closer.
Panther wiped off some of the mud and held it up.
It was beautiful.
"I think it's a seashell," she replied.
She began wiping off the rest of the mud.
Suddenly the shell began to giggle.
Panther was so shocked she almost dropped it.
"It laughed!" Bobby shouted loudly.
"Something's inside." He knocked on the shell.
"Ouch! Stop that!" the shell cried.
The children all looked at each other.
Then the most amazing thing happened.
A creature poked its head out from the shell.
It had the face of a seahorse.
On its neck and back were shimmery fins that opened and closed.
As its head circled left and right, the fins glowed and shone.
For the first time in their lives, the children were speechless.
"Well?" the creature asked in an irritated voice.
Finally, Panther spoke up.
"What are you?"
The creature gazed at them.
"Let me get this straight," it began.
"You throw things on me and wake me up."
It glared at Jane.
"You start taking away my things."
It looked at Cy.
"You tickle me."
It stared at Panther.
"Then you bang on my shell!"
Bobby looked down at the ground.
"And now, you tell me that you don't even know what I am?"
The children stared at the ground in embarrassment.
"We're sorry," apologized Jane.
"We didn't know you were in the well."
The creature didn't say anything.
After a while, its fins stopped glowing.
"Apology accepted," it said finally.
"But we really don't know what you are," Cy added quickly.
"I am Huit des Orlanes," it announced.
"The eighth of my kind of the sea."
"Wow," the children said in unison.
"But you can call me Huey," the creature smiled.
It was clear from the children's blank faces that they still did not know what he was.
"Do you know what an Orlane is?" he asked.
"Not really," Jane admitted for them all.
Huey closed his eyes dramatically.
His head turned quickly from side to side.
"At one time," he said, "we Orlanes were the best-known mystic creatures of the sea."
"You mean, you're a fairy?" interrupted Bobby.
"A fairy? Oh, my, oh, my!"
Huey's fins started to glow again as they opened and closed quickly.
"Please don't be upset, Huey," said Jane.
"Bobby didn't mean to call you a fairy."
"All right then," Huey said calmly.
"Orlanes have the gift to grant others whatever they want," he continued.
"You mean you can make wishes come true?" Bobby asked.
Huey nodded, and the other children joined Bobby in shouts of delight.
"However," Huey said in a loud voice.
"There are two things you must promise."
"We'll do anything to get our wish!" Jane clapped her hands.
Huey continued. "First," he said, "you can only make one wish a day.
And second, after making your wish, you must return me to the well."
"That doesn't sound too hard." Cy laughed.
"By the way," Huey smiled, "at sunset, everything returns to the way it was."
"You mean, our wish is true only for one day?" asked Bobby in a disappointed voice.
"Yes," Huey replied, and with that he disappeared back into his shell.
The Barth children could not recognize each other.
"Cy?" Panther asked, reaching out to a young boy with dark, wavy hair and clear blue eyes.
"Panther?" Cy said.
He touched a long wavy lock of her golden hair.
Panther's hair was normally straight brown and quite plain.
"Does anyone have a mirror?" asked Jane.
"What do I look like?"
Jane was absolutely beautiful.
She had short red hair with little curls around her face.
Her skin was rosy, and she had bright, shining green eyes.
"I don't know why anyone wants to be beautiful," complained Bobby,
"This was your idea, wasn't it, Panther?"
"Yes, I wished it," admitted Panther,
"but I'm glad to be beautiful for once."
"Good, lovely, and all that," Huey interrupted.
"Now, be off with you.
Remember that your wish ends at sunset."
Huey disappeared back into his shell.
Cy carefully lowered him back down the well.
The children walked into town.
Many people turned to stare at them.
"I must be beautiful because everyone is looking at me," thought Panther.
Just then, she recognized Aunt Martha's neighbor.
"Look! There's Mr. Becker," she said.
Mr. Becker was walking his dog, Silver.
"Hello, Mr. Becker! Hello, Silver!" Panther called out cheerfully.
Panther, being an animal lover, had gottten to know Silver as soon as they had arrived at Aunt Martha's.
Now, however, neither Mr. Becker nor Silver seemed to recognize her.
"Woof! Woof!" Silver barked angrily.
"What's the matter, Silver? It's me, Panther!" she said.
Panther bent down to pet the dog's head.
"Be careful, young lady," Mr. Becker warned.
"Or else my dog might bite your hand."
Bobby faced his neighbor.
"Mr. Becker, it's Bobby Barth!" he said.
"We live next door."
Mr. Becker looked at each child suspiciously.
"I don't know who you children are," he said in a stern voice.
"But I've never seen you before in my life."
"But, but . . ." Panther stepped forward, attempting to explain.
Suddenly, Silver lunged.
Quickly Panther stepped back, but Silver had pulled the leash from Mr. Becker's hand.
Startled, the children all turned and fled.
Excitedly, the barking dog gave chase.
"Run!" yelled Cy.
The children ran toward their aunt's house.
"I hope Aunt Martha is home!" gasped Panther.
Luckily for the children, the front door was open.
"Hurry!" Cy shouted to his siblings.
He slammed the door behind them, just as Silver reached the steps.
The children collapsed onto the floor.
"That was a close call," Bobby sighed loudly.
"Why did Silver chase me?
He loves me!"
wailed Panther, her beautiful eyes filling with tears.
"Because you look different,"
Cy pointed out, but it didn't help Panther feel much better.
The children looked all over for Aunt Martha and Lamb.
"She's not home,"
said Cy, as everyone followed him into the kitchen.
"Maybe she went shopping?" said Jane.
"Well, I'm hungry," Bobby said.
"I'm going to have a snack."
He opened the fridge.
"I'm taking a shower," said Cy, heading for the stairs.
"Come on, Panther." Jane held out her hand.
"Let's go get changed."
Panther took a moment to study her brothers and sister.
Their voices sounded the same.
But when Panther looked at their faces, it felt as if she was in a house with strangers.

episodes.title: All That Glitters Is Not Gold

subtitle.text: The children decided to go home and put their riches into bags.
Cy and Bobby put all their gold coins into a backpack.
"How will I know which ones are mine?" asked Bobby.
"It doesn't matter," replied his brother.
"We can share."
The girls decided to divide their money.
"Panther, that's my gold coin,"
Jane said, grabbing a coin that fell to the floor.
"No, Jane. It's mine.
It fell out of my pocket," argued Panther.
She snatched the coin from her little sister and put it into her bag.
In town, the children were excited by their new wealth.
"What are you going to buy first?" Bobby asked Cy.
"I'm going to get a hundred games so I won't ever be bored," he answered.
"I'm going to buy a car,"
Bobby said with a sparkle in his eye.
"You can't drive," Jane pointed out.
Bobby shrugged and said, "Doesn't matter.
I'll get a driver to drive me around."
Cy stopped in front of a store.
"Here we are," he said.
He lifted his hand toward the sign that read "Game World."
"I don't want to go in that store," said Bobby.
"Me neither," agreed Jane.
"I'm going to Dot's Dress Shop to look at skirts," said Panther.
The children began to argue about where to go first.
Finally Cy raised both hands and said,
"We can all go wherever we want.
We'll meet here after we've been shopping, okay?"
The others quickly agreed.
Cy walked into the game store alone.
His eyes fell on the rows and rows of games.
"Wow!" he said, sucking in his breath.
"Can I help you?" asked the store clerk.
"Yes," Cy answered.
"I want one of every game in the store."
Meanwhile, Bobby went to look at cars.
He fingered a two-door silver sports car.
"Are you looking for a birthday gift for your dad?" one car salesman teased.
"Maybe he's saving up to buy it in ten years," laughed another.
"More like twenty years," roared the other.
Bobby held his head high and left the store.
"They'll see," he thought.
Panther and Jane went to Dot's Dress Shop to buy some clothes.
The girls tried on many dresses and found one that they liked.
"Jane, that's my dress,"
said Panther, pointing to the dress Jane was trying on.
It was exactly the same one that Panther had on.
"It's my dress.
I saw it first," Jane replied hotly.
"Why don't you find another dress?" Panther said sweetly.
"Why don't you?" Jane replied nastily.
Back at the game store, Cy stood at the checkout.
He was counting all the new games that were soon to be his.
"Look, boy," said the clerk, "how are you going to pay for all this?"
"I happen to be a very rich man," Cy replied snobbishly.
"Maybe you should show me the money first,"
the clerk said, rolling his eyes.
Cy threw the heavy backpack of gold coins onto the counter.
"This bag is full of money," he told the clerk.
"Cy!" Bobby said, suddenly running into the store.
"I need some money for my car."
Cy pushed his brother away.
"Not now, Bobby. I'm busy!" he said.
"But I found the car I want!" Bobby said.
He tried to grab the bag.
Cy shoved Bobby.
"I'll give it to you after I pay for my games!" he said.
"It's my money too!" yelled Bobby.
Cy and Bobby held on to each other as they fell faster to the ground.
"Bobby," cried Cy, "flap your wings.
Keep them moving!"
Soon the brothers regained control.
They flew over to their sisters.
"That was a close call," Cy said in a trembling voice.
Panther looked around.
She spotted a large tree branch.
"Let's rest over there."
As the children flew toward the tree, Jane suddenly asked:
"How do we land?"
"The wings have to fold back like an umbrella," Panther said after a while.
"Let me try."
Panther flew to the tree.
One of her wings folded.
The other, however, got caught in the leaves.
"Ouch!" she cried.
The other children followed after her.
Cy landed gracefully, and so did Bobby.
"We made it!" the brothers exclaimed, grinning.
Jane, however, did not want to rest.
"We don't have much time," she said.
"I want to fly as much as I can."
She lifted her head and flew higher.
"We'd better stay together," said Panther.
So the others flew after Jane.
The children flew over lakes and mountains.
Birds squawked loudly as the children flew by.
After a while, Bobby said, "I'm hungry."
"But where can we get food?" Panther wondered aloud.
"We can't walk around with these things," said Cy.
He pointed to his wings.
It would be impossible to hide their wings.
The children searched high and low for food.
But they could not find anything.
"I know where we might find food," said Cy.
"Farmer Jenkins makes his own jam."
Farmer Jenkins was Aunt Martha's neighbor.
Sometimes he gave Aunt Martha homemade bread and jam.
"You mean steal his food?" shouted Panther.
Cy's face turned red.
"Not steal it. Just borrow it."
"That's a terrible idea," scolded Panther.
"Do you have any better ones?" Cy shot back.
Of course Panther did not have any ideas at all.
"Well, if you promise to return what we take," she finally agreed.
"Okay, just follow me."
Cy turned around and flew off.
By the time they reached the farm, it was late afternoon.
"He probably keeps his food in the barn," said Cy.
The barn had two floors.
Luckily, a large window on the second level was open.
The children flew in through that window.
Cy found several wooden boxes.
They were filled with jam.
Without a word, the children ate the jam.
"That was delicious," Bobby said, licking his lips.
"We must remember how much we ate,"
said Panther as she counted the empty jars.
"Look! The sun is setting!"
Jane pointed to the glowing red sky.
Suddenly the children felt lighter, as if a weight had been lifted off their shoulders.
"They're gone," whispered Jane, reaching around to touch her flat back.
"Well, we have to get out of here now," Cy said.
Without wings, the children could not fly out.
The main door was on the ground floor.
The animals were kept down there.
"We can climb down this ladder," said Cy.
In the middle of the floor was a large square opening.
There was a ladder inside the opening.
Cy got on the ladder.
"Come on," Cy said as he climbed down.
As each child climbed down, the animals grew noisier.
"Hush," Panther whispered to a particularly loud horse.
Cy headed for the barn entrance.
He pulled the door.
It wouldn't move.
He tried again.
Cy looked at his siblings with wide eyes.
"It's locked."
Everyone except Cy was stunned.
Even Lamb grew quiet.
"Did you say dinosaurs?" repeated Bobby.
"I've always wanted to see a real one," Cy explained.
Huey cleared his throat and pointed to the well.
"But my wish hasn't come true yet," argued Cy.
Crossing his arms, Huey asked,
"Has any wish not come true so far?"
The children admitted that every wish had indeed come true.
"This one will too."
Huey disappeared into his shell.
Cy lowered him down, mumbling, "I don't see any dinosaurs."
"Patience!" Huey yelled from his shell.
"Let's go home," Cy said in a disappointed voice.
The children started to walk back home.
But something was different.
"I've never seen this tree before."
Jane pointed to a tall leafy tree.
"This road looks unfamiliar,"
Panther remarked, holding Lamb close to her.
"Why is that tree moving?"
Bobby took steps behind his brother.
The leaves on one tree swayed side to side.
Then the children felt the ground tremble.
"Something's coming this way," whispered Cy excitedly.
"What is it?" Jane asked, close to tears.
Suddenly a huge dinosaur with many horns appeared among the trees.
"It's a rhino," Bobby said in awe.
The huge dinosaur did resemble a rhinoceros in many ways.
But it was much bigger and scarier.
"No, that's not a rhino," Cy corrected.
"That's a Centrosaurus."
The Centrosaurus did not know the children were watching him.
He continued to eat the leaves off the trees and plants.
"Is he dangerous?" Jane said in a tiny voice.
Cy nodded. "But if we don't bother him, we would be safe."
"So Huey gave you your wish," said Panther.
At that moment, the Centrosaurus lifted his head and sniffed the air.
He grunted loudly and pawed the ground.
"Uh-oh," said Cy, "I think he can smell us."
"What do we do?" asked Bobby.
"Everybody move back slowly.
Slowly now," Cy said in a calm voice.
The children stepped back deeper into the woods.
Safely away from the dinosaur, Cy jumped up in excitement.
"This must be the Cretaceous period," he said.
"These dinosaurs lived over 130 million years ago."
The children's eyes grew wide with interest─except for Lamb's.
His eyes were getting heavy.
"It's his nap time," Panther whispered.
Lamb was soon fast asleep in her arms.
Cy found a safe, dry spot under a tree.
Panther gently placed Lamb there.
"Let's go see more dinosaurs," Cy said.
"We can't leave him," argued Panther.
"We won't go far," said Cy.
"Just around that tree."
Panther admitted that seeing the giant creatures was very fascinating.
She kept a close eye on Lamb but followed Cy.
"That one is an iguanodon,"
Cy said, pointing to a creature with a long, stiff tail.
"That one has a duck's bill," giggled Jane.
She indicated a tall dinosaur with short arms.
"That's a Corythosaurus," Cy said.
"It looks like he's wearing a helmet."
Bobby laughed aloud.
He was referring to the crest on its head.
The children would have watched the dinosaurs longer, but something terrible had happened.
"Cy, where's Lamb?" Panther cried.
They looked back where Lamb had been sleeping.
But he was gone.
Panther would not stop crying.
"It's all my fault," she kept repeating.
"We're going to find him," comforted Cy.
As the children searched, Bobby discovered something interesting.
"Footprints!" he shouted.
Cy studied the prints carefully.
Then he said, "This creature can walk on two or four legs."
"A dinosaur took Lamb?
What if he eats him?" asked Jane, worried.
"We can't waste anymore time."
Cy followed the footprints.
They led them deeper into the forest.
They looked everywhere but still found no sign of Lamb.
Exhausted, the children leaned against a tree.
"What are we going to do now?" sniffed Panther.
Suddenly the ground began to shake.
The children glanced at each other.
They were afraid.
The ground trembled again.
"Something really big is coming," said Bobby.
Then they heard the most frightful scream.
The hairs on their necks stood up.
"Uh-oh," muttered Cy.
"What is it?" whispered Jane.
The trembling became more intense.
"Run!" shouted Cy.
The children took off in the opposite direction from the noise.
"Don't look back," Cy yelled at the top of his voice.
But it was too late.
Bobby turned around to see what was chasing them.
"It's a T. rex!" he screamed.
Then he tripped and fell hard to the ground.
The Tyrannosaurus rex was a gigantic creature with extremely sharp teeth.
It looked very angry and mean.
And it was getting closer to where Bobby lay.
"Bobby! Get up!" screamed Panther.
But Bobby could not move.
Just then the T. rex stopped.
It looked behind the children.
Then it let out another fierce, threatening cry.
The children covered their ears to block out the terrifying noises.
Brave Cy kept his eyes open to see what made the king of dinosaurs stop.
Right behind them a massive Triceratops had appeared.
The three-horned monster was lowering its head.
It was getting ready to attack.
"The T. rex and Triceratops are going to fight!
Get out! Get out!"
Cy screamed to his siblings.
Somehow the children made it to safety.
"Are they going to kill each other?" cried Jane.
"That's how dinosaurs survive, Jane."
Cy tried to comfort his sister.
"Right now we have to think about Lamb."
The children kept running.
"Ahhh!" Bobby suddenly yelled.
"Ahhh! Be careful!" Panther's cries followed.
Cy and Jane should have listened to their sister.
But they kept running.
Soon they fell into a large hole in the ground, just as Bobby and Panther had done.
It was about two meters deep.
"It looks like some kind of nest," observed Panther.
She picked up a smooth oval-shaped egg.
It was the size of a big grapefruit.
There were at least twenty eggs.
"You mean," gasped Jane, "we're in a dinosaur's nest?"
"It looks that way," replied Cy.
"Dada?" a baby's voice called from among the eggs.
"Lamb!" Panther cried with joy.
Somehow Lamb had ended up in this dinosaur's nest.
"Are you okay?" Panther fussed over her brother.
"Mama!" Lamb smiled and pointed behind Panther.
Panther turned around and screamed.
A dinosaur was heading toward the nest.
She looked very angry.
"That's a Maiasaura," Cy said, trembling.
"She thinks we're trying to harm her babies."
The dinosaur's strong tail swung back and forth.
Her sharp claws were ready to attack.
Huey's fins opened and closed.
They shone all different colors.
But he was quiet.
"What's the matter, Huey?" asked Jane.
"I've never said anything before," he said, "but are you sure this is what you want?"
Huey looked really worried.
"I don't like being a child," Jane said.
"People always tell you what to do.
But grown-ups can do whatever they want."
Huey shook his head.
"No, Jane. Being grown-up is harder than you think.
But this is your wish."
His fins turned dark.
Then the children felt a tickling in their arms and legs.
"I'm growing!" Bobby shouted.
His chubby stomach disappeared as he continued to grow tall.
"Look at me!" shouted Jane.
Her hair turned darker as she also grew taller.
Panther's glasses disappeared and her face grew longer.
Not only did Cy grow taller but he also got bigger.
His stomach stuck out in front of him.
"Cy's fat!" teased Bobby.
"Shut up, Bobby," Cy yelled back.
Finally the tickling feeling stopped.
They had stopped growing.
Now the children were no longer children.
"You are all grown-up," Huey said sadly.
They looked at each other.
Cy and Bobby were wearing suits.
"This tie is choking me," complained Bobby.
Panther and Jane were wearing skirts and high heels.
They carried purses.
"I'm a woman!" Jane said happily.
"Well, my work is done.
So if you'd please . . ." Huey pointed to the well.
Grown-up Cy lowered the bucket more quickly than ever.
"Wow! That was fast," he said.
"That's because you're bigger," Jane said.
"We've all changed," Panther remarked.
But it was different from the first wish.
When they had been beautiful, they had looked like strangers to one another.
"I can recognize you," continued Panther.
"But you look . . ."
"What, Panther?" asked Jane.
"You look old," Panther said.
"What's done is done.
Let's go into town," said Cy.
The adult Barths walked through the woods.
It was not a comfortable journey for any of them.
"This tie is too tight!"
Bobby continued to complain.
"I can't walk in these heels," cried Panther.
"This suit jacket is making me hot," said Cy.
"I keep dropping my purse," said Jane.
They were relieved to finally get to town.
Other adults looked at them as they passed.
"Good morning," Cy called out in a grown-up voice.
"Good morning," people answered back.
"Wow! They think we're one of them!" he whispered to his siblings.
"I feel so important," Bobby said, standing up taller.
"What do you want to do?" asked Panther.
"I know," said Jane, her eyes shining brightly.
"Let's get coffee!"
The children always wondered what coffee tasted like.
Their parents and Aunt Martha drank it every morning.
"Coffee is for grown-ups," Mom had always said.
"Wait till you're older," Dad used to say.
The grown-up Barths found a small coffee shop.
They walked up to the counter and ordered four large coffees.
"Hey, Cy, can I have some cheesecake?" asked Bobby.
"You know what Mom said about sweets," Cy replied.
The man behind the counter looked at them strangely.
"Will there be anything else?" he asked.
"Uh, no, that's all," Cy said in his new, deep voice.
The children took the coffee to a table near the window.
As soon as they sat down, Jane took off her heels.
"How can anyone walk in those?" she complained, rubbing her feet.
"Yuck!" Panther spit out the coffee she drank.
"This is disgusting!
How can Mom and Dad like this?"
The other children tried it, too.
"It tastes awful," agreed Cy.
The grown-up Barths wondered why adults drank that bitter black stuff.
When the Barths got home, it was getting dark.
"I don't ever want to grow up,"
Jane said, her lips trembling.
"Growing up is not the problem," Panther said kindly.
"It's growing up too fast.
We weren't ready."
"Well, I think people here are just mean," said Bobby.
"In Chicago, nobody would have said nasty things."
"You don't know that, Bobby," said Cy.
"Yes, I do.
This town is full of mean people.
And it's so boring!" Bobby continued.
"If it weren't for Huey, we would have nothing to do."
The children agreed with him on that.
"I think today's wish was a good lesson for us," said Panther.
"At least we know what we're going to look like,"
laughed Cy as he patted his stomach.
Suddenly the Barths felt the same tickling feeling they had felt that morning.
Their arms and legs got shorter.
Cy's stomach disappeared while Bobby's reappeared.
Within a few minutes, the Barths were once again children.
"It's good to be me again," said Jane.
They gave each other hugs.
"Let's go inside and have something to eat," said Panther.
During dinner, Aunt Martha told them about her day.
"I took Lamb to the park," she said.
"We saw these adults running around behaving like children."
"Maybe they just wanted to have fun," Cy said in quiet voice.
"Having fun is no problem.
But people should act their age!" Aunt Martha said.
The children looked at each other.
"I agree with Aunt Martha," said Jane.
"We should act our age."
The next morning, the children got ready to go out.
Aunt Martha took Lamb outside to the garden.
"It's your turn, Bobby," whispered Cy.
"I don't have a wish," he said.
"Can I do it tomorrow?"
The others thought about it.
Then Panther said, "We can all use a break."
"So today we won't go see Huey," said Cy.
Panther read a book.
Jane played with her dolls.
Cy went for a bike ride.
And Bobby did nothing.
He didn't want to go outside.
He hated reading.
He didn't want to play with his toys.
"It's so boring here," he kept saying.
"Why don't you do something then?" said Panther.
"There's nothing to do.
This town is so boring!" he complained.
"I miss Chicago.
Something exciting always happens there."
"Bobby, we've had so many adventures lately," said Panther.
"And you're still bored?"
"I want something exciting to happen here!
Here in this town," said Bobby with feeling.
Panther rolled her eyes and returned to her book.
Suddenly Bobby sat up and snapped his fingers.
"That's it!" he shouted.
"I know what I'm going to wish for."
The next day, Bobby was in a better mood.
"It was nice not having a wish yesterday," said Cy.
"Yeah, I finally finished my book," said Panther.
"I didn't have to worry about dinosaurs.
Or mean people," giggled Jane.
"Well, I'm ready to make my wish today," Bobby said excitedly.
For some reason, the others did not feel as eager.
But they went to Huey's well.
When Cy pulled him up, Huey did not come out right away.
They had to tap lightly on his shell.
"Oh, it's you! I thought you weren't coming back,"
Huey said when he appeared.
Cy explained that they hadn't come up with a wish the previous day.
"But today I have," beamed Bobby.
"I wish," he said dramatically, "that something exciting would happen in our town."
Bobby and his siblings walked back home.
So far everything seemed the same.
"What exciting thing were you thinking of?" asked Panther.
"Anything! I don't care." Bobby shrugged.
When they got home, Aunt Martha was on her way out.
"I need to run to the bank," she said.
"Can we come with you?" asked Jane.
"Jane!" hissed Bobby.
He wanted to wait for his wish to come true.
"Of course," Aunt Martha said.
"Then we can get new shoes for Lamb."
"Shoes?" Bobby almost shouted.
This day did not sound exciting at all.
The children walked with Aunt Martha to the bank.
Bobby walked behind the others and dragged his feet.
The guard at the bank greeted them.
"Good morning, everyone."
"Good morning," they said in return.
The bank was quite busy that morning.
Aunt Martha, holding Lamb, went to stand in line.
"You can wait for me on those benches," she told the children.
The children sat on hard wooden benches.
They looked around.
Bobby noticed Mr. Keefer, the shop owner.
He also saw Mr. Becker.
Bobby glanced outside.
Mr. Becker's dog, Silver, was tied to a fire hydrant.
At that moment, four men stopped in front of the bank.
They looked nervous.
One man had a scar on his face.
Another man had a ponytail.
"I wonder if they're lost," Bobby said aloud.
Then quick as lightning, they pulled masks over their heads.
Bobby opened his mouth but no sounds came out.
The men entered the bank holding guns.
"Ladies and gentlemen," one man said in a calm voice.
The bank customers turned around.
When they saw the masked men, some began screaming.
"Everybody, stay calm.
Do not scream!" the man said, holding his gun up.
Meanwhile, another man tied the guard's hands behind his back.
He put tape over his mouth, too.
A third man locked the bank doors.
He rushed around pulling down the blinds.
The fourth man jumped behind the tellers.
"Do not push the alarm!" he warned them.
"I want everyone to move here," the first man said.
He pointed to where the children sat.
"And lie down on the floor."
"Please, there are children here," a woman cried.
It was Aunt Martha.
"Quiet!" the first man shouted.
He was probably the leader.
"If they behave," he said, turning to look at the Barth children, "nobody will get hurt."
Everybody obeyed the robber's instructions.
They walked to where the children sat.
Then they dropped to the floor.
Aunt Martha motioned for the children to lie on the ground as well.
From the floor, Bobby could see only the robbers' feet.
Two of the men wore sneakers.
One of the sneakers had a large hole in it.
Bobby could see the socks of the man wearing it.
They were blue with red stripes.
"Put all your money and jewelry in this bag."
The robber with blue socks dropped a bag in front of the people.
They removed their purses and wallets.
Some took off their watches.
The robbers also took rings, necklaces, and earrings.
Bobby lifted his head slightly.
Behind the counter, the tellers opened their registers.
"Hurry up," the fourth man said, holding the gun close to them.
"Well, Bobby," Cy whispered to him, "your wish came true."
Lying on the floor was very uncomfortable.
"Are you okay?" a man whispered to Bobby.
It was Farmer Jenkins.
"Everything's going to be fine," he assured Bobby.
"I want everyone to close their eyes," the leader shouted.
"Then start counting to one hundred."
Everyone did exactly as he said.
Bobby heard heavy footsteps.
Then he heard a door opening somewhere.
"They're gone!" a woman said loudly.
" . . . fifty-seven, fifty-eight . . . "
Jane kept counting, her eyes still closed.
Panther gently tapped her.
"It's over, Jane," she said.
People started to get up slowly and carefully.
Police sirens rang loudly outside.
Soon police officers and an ambulance crew crowded the bank.
"Did anybody see anything?" an officer called out.
Most of the people shook their heads.
"They wore masks," one man said.
Bobby raised his hand.
"Did you see something, son?" the officer asked Bobby.
"Yes, sir," Bobby answered timidly.
The officer put his hand on Bobby's shoulder and said,
"Tell me what you saw."
Bobby described the men before they entered the bank.
He also told the officer about the socks he'd noticed on one of the men.
"I didn't see their faces though," he said.
The officer gave Bobby a big smile.
"This is going to help us find them."
Bobby's chest swelled with pride.
"Aren't you Martha's nieces and nephews?"
A woman wearing a yellow sweater approached them.
The children nodded.
"You were very brave throughout this incident," she commended.
The children smiled shyly.
"I agree." Mr. Becker came over to them as well.
A few hours later, the police allowed everyone to return home.
Many people, however, did not want to go home.
"Nothing like this has happened before," Mr. Keefer said angrily.
"We must catch those robbers," Mr. Becker said with feeling.
"But what can we do?" asked Aunt Martha.
"We should all work together to protect our town," said Mr. Keefer.
People nodded in agreement.
Aunt Martha invited everyone to her house for tea.
"We can think better after a drink," she said.
The children helped Aunt Martha prepare the tea.
They also brought out some cookies.
"Thank you."
"You're so sweet."
"What good manners you have!"
People kept complimenting the children.
"Everyone is so nice,"
Panther said when they were alone in the kitchen.
"One woman said I look like her granddaughter," beamed Jane.
"Mr. Becker wants us to come over for dinner," said Cy.
Bobby was also beginning to like his neighbors.
"Children," Aunt Martha came into the kitchen.
"Can you get more bread for me?" she asked.
Cy and Bobby volunteered to go.
Handing them some money, Aunt Martha said,
"Hurry back and be careful!"
The boys left the house and ran over to the bakery.
"I heard you were at the bank," the baker said to them.
The baker asked many questions.
Some of the customers did too.
"Well," the baker said finally, "you were very brave.
I hope they catch those robbers."
Cy took out the money to pay for the bread.
"How much is this?"
The baker shook his head.
"No, this is on me.
For you brave children."
Thanking him, the boys ran out.
"Oomph!" Bobby ran right into a man walking by.
Bobby fell hard on the ground.
"Watch where you're going, kid!" he yelled at Bobby.
"Are you okay?" Cy asked, pulling Bobby up.
"Cy!" Bobby grabbed his brother's arm.
"Look at that man's shoes!"
The man was about to cross the street.
One of his shoes had a hole in it.
And he wore blue socks with red stripes.
